alignment.note: Greek uses the single negative interrogative particle οὐχ expecting an affirmative answer; the Peshitta renders this with the two-word expression ܠܐ ܗܘܐ ('is not this'), employing the verb ܗܘܐ as a copular element. Latin Nonne is the standard rhetorical-question particle, semantically equivalent to all.
Greek ἐστιν and Latin est supply the explicit copula; the Syriac copular force is already carried by ܗܘܐ in the preceding group, so no separate token corresponds here.

Greek ὁ τέκτων and Latin faber both denote a craftsman/carpenter with the definite article (Greek) or anarthrous noun (Latin); Syriac ܢܓܪܐ (root n-g-r) is the cognate term for carpenter, the article being implicit in the emphatic state.

Greek expresses 'the son' analytically with article plus noun (ὁ υἱός); Latin filius is anarthrous; Syriac compresses 'son of' into the single construct form ܒܪܗ with pronominal suffix, a synthetic construction equivalent in sense.
Μαρίας / ܕܡܪܝܡ / Mariæ — the proper name of Mary in genitive; the Syriac form preserves the Semitic vocalisation ܡܪܝܡ (Maryam).

Greek joins with καί … δέ (a doubled connective, 'and … moreover') before ἀδελφός; the Peshitta fuses conjunction and noun into ܘܐܚܘܗܝ ('and his brother', with suffix); Latin uses bare frater without conjunction. The connective particles differ but the relational sense is identical.
Ἰακώβου / ܕܝܥܩܘܒ / Jacobi — James in the genitive.
καὶ Ἰωσῆτος / ܘܕܝܘܣܐ / et Joseph — 'and of Joses/Joseph'; the Syriac fuses conjunction and name into one token, Latin and Greek keep them separate.
καὶ Ἰούδα / ܘܕܝܗܘܕܐ / et Judæ — 'and of Judas'; Syriac again contracts conjunction and name.
καὶ Σίμωνος / ܘܕܫܡܥܘܢ / et Simonis — 'and of Simon'; the Latin closes the first question with a question mark (idx 14), and the Greek marks it with the high point on Σίμωνος.

Greek opens the second rhetorical question with καὶ οὐκ ('and not'); the Peshitta uses the fused ܘܠܐ ('and not'); Latin restates the full interrogative particle nonne plus et. All convey the negative question expecting affirmation.

The Peshitta inserts the presentative particle ܗܐ ('behold/lo') introducing the sisters, a feature absent from both the Greek NA28 and the Vulgate. This is a characteristic Syriac discourse marker heightening the rhetorical force of the question.

Greek has article + noun + genitive pronoun (αἱ ἀδελφαὶ αὐτοῦ, 'his sisters'); Latin sorores ejus is anarthrous; Syriac ܐܚܘܬܗ synthesises 'sisters' plus the third-person suffix into a single construct form. The possessive sense is uniform.
Greek uses preposition plus pronoun πρὸς ἡμᾶς ('with us'); Latin renders idiomatically with the enclitic ablative nobiscum; Syriac fuses preposition and suffix into ܠܘܬܢ. All express 'among/with us'.

Greek places the copula εἰσὶν ('they are') early in the clause (idx 21) following οὐκ; Latin defers sunt to clause-final position and supplies a closing question mark. The Syriac second clause is verbless, relying on the ܗܐ + emphatic-state construction, so no copular token aligns there.
καί / Et — the narrative connective 'and' introducing the consequence; the Syriac fuses this conjunction into the following verb form ܘܡܬܟܫܠܝܢ.

Greek uses a single imperfect ἐσκανδαλίζοντο ('they were taking offence'); Latin scandalizabantur is the direct Latinised cognate imperfect; Syriac employs a periphrastic construction ܘܡܬܟܫܠܝܢ ܗܘܘ (participle + auxiliary ܗܘܘ, root k-sh-l 'to stumble') to express the durative past, the normal Syriac equivalent of the Greek imperfect.
ἐν αὐτῷ / ܒܗ / in illo — 'at/by him'; Syriac fuses preposition ܒ and suffix into ܒܗ. The Greek paragraph marker ¶ here functions only as editorial punctuation.
